notes: Confiscation appeal on benefit fraud; Court of Appeal rejects notional WFTC offset and section 71(1C) civil proceedings argument.

enrichment.short_title: R v Richards: confiscation order and notional Working Families Tax Credit offset
key_facts: Mr Richards dishonestly claimed income support for about three and a half years after he and his partner began working, overpaying the state £22,735.19.
He pleaded guilty to specimen benefit fraud offences and received concurrent four-month sentences plus a confiscation order of £19,424.30 after allowance for Family Credit and voluntary repayments.
He argued the confiscation benefit should be reduced by a notional £16,521 Working Families Tax Credit entitlement and that section 71(1C) applied because the DWP had civil recovery proceedings.
The trial judge followed R (Larusai) v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions and refused to treat tax credits as an offset against benefit overpayments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave of a single judge against a Crown Court confiscation order made after conviction for social security fraud.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; notional tax credit could not reduce confiscated benefit and the DWP recovery scheme did not constitute civil proceedings for section 71(1C) purposes.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 71(4) benefit is measured by property or pecuniary advantage obtained at the time of the offence, not by hypothetical honest returns; notional tax credit is not a debt owed by the victim and section 71(1C) requires instituted civil proceedings by way of claim form, not statutory overpayment recovery.
legal_issues: Whether notional Working Families Tax Credit should reduce benefit for confiscation purposes
Whether section 71(1C) conferred discretion because the DWP sought overpayment recovery
Construction of benefit under section 71(4) following R v May
Whether a statutory recovery regime amounts to civil proceedings
linked_authorities: R (on the application of Larusai) v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions [2003] EWHC 371 (Admin)
R v May [2005] EWCA Crim 97
R v Roissetter [2004] EWCA Crim 1827

notes: Second habeas corpus application in Swiss extradition; Maurice Kay J dismissed speciality/bad faith challenge.

enrichment.short_title: Sutej v Governor HMP Holloway: second habeas corpus on Swiss fraud extradition
key_facts: Ingrid Sutej was committed for extradition to Switzerland on 27 fraud charges relating mainly to George Rafael after the Court of Appeal discharged four Nina Brink charges in July 2003.
Her second habeas corpus application argued the Swiss Investigating Magistrate M Tappolet showed bad faith by retaining Brink material and intending to revisit those allegations after return.
Correspondence showed Tappolet would decide partie civile status only after Sutej's return and declined to purge his file of Brink documents.
The Secretary of State had not yet ordered return on the remaining Rafael charges.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second habeas corpus application challenging continued custody pending extradition to Switzerland on the Rafael charges.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed with costs of £1,700; the magistrate's correspondence did not manifest bad faith or an intention to breach speciality protection.
enrichment.ratio: Extradition proceedings do not resolve trial issues abroad; section 11(3)(c) requires evidence of bad faith on the balance of probabilities, and a foreign investigating magistrate's wait-and-see stance on related allegations does not show an intention to disregard Article 14 speciality protection.
legal_issues: Whether M Tappolet's retention of Brink material breached the speciality rule
Whether accusations were made in good faith under section 11(3)(c)
Construction of 'accusation' to include foreign court conduct
Whether Swiss criminal procedure differences justify discharge
linked_authorities: Kashanu v Governor of Brixton Prison [2002] 2 WLR 907
Davison [1983] 77 Cr App R 309
Ex parte Ross Munro [1967] 1 QB 620

notes: Contempt committal hearing on breach of court undertakings by employee joining rival poultry distributor; financial penalty only.

enrichment.short_title: Westbridge Foods v Radovits: contempt for breach of employment undertakings
key_facts: Tamas Radovits gave undertakings on 9 October 2003 not to solicit Westbridge customers or suppliers, not to work for a competitor, and to act in good faith while still employed by Westbridge Foods.
He had accepted work with rival distributor Oakfield and, during the undertaking period, traded on Oakfield's behalf with suppliers and customers including S & A Foods, THP, Bomadek and Carnex.
He gave misleading affidavits before admitting extensive breaches; telephone and computer records exposed covert Oakfield activity.
The substantive action settled for £85,000 but the committal application proceeded on multiple pleaded breaches.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court committal hearing after trial of alleged contempt for breach of consent-order undertakings; penalty and costs reserved then determined.
enrichment.outcome: Contempt proved on admitted and found breaches; no imprisonment ordered; financial penalty of £1,800 and £25,000 costs on account ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Breaches of undertakings not to work for a competitor and to act in good faith may amount to contempt where proved to the criminal standard; deliberate evasion and false affidavits aggravate contempt but late frank admissions and elapsed time may justify a financial rather than custodial penalty.
legal_issues: Whether particularised allegations of breach were proved beyond reasonable doubt
Whether Oakfield was a competitor within the undertaking
Construction of the good faith obligation
Appropriate penalty for sustained deliberate breach of court undertakings
linked_authorities: Faccenda Chicken Ltd v Fowler [1987] 1 Ch 117
Johnson v Walton [1990] 1 FLR 350
Hivac Ltd v Park Royal Scientific Instruments Ltd [1946] 1 Ch 169

notes: Libel summary judgment appeal dismissed in absentia; Sedley LJ upheld Eady J on Defamation Act 1996 and Article 6.

enrichment.short_title: Steinberg v Pritchard Englefield: libel summary judgment appeal dismissed in absentia
key_facts: Mr Steinberg, a US-qualified barrister, sued solicitors Pritchard Englefield and Mr Cohn over a letter alleging inflated costs accessible via search engines and his website.
Eady J gave summary judgment under sections 8-10 of the Defamation Act 1996 after adjournments for medical and financial evidence, awarding £5,000 damages but costs exceeded £191,000.
Steinberg appealed in absentia relying on lack of representation, stress, and Steel and Morris on Article 6 legal aid.
The ECHR had already declared his Convention complaint inadmissible in October 2004.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against summary judgment and case management decisions in a defamation claim; heard in the appellant's absence after repeated adjournments.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; costs assessed at £25,000; court held Eady J was entitled to proceed to summary judgment and no realistic defence existed.
enrichment.ratio: Sections 8-10 summary disposal does not breach Article 6 where no defence has a realistic prospect of success; indefinite unavailability and impecuniosity do not require adjournment, and Steel and Morris does not establish a general right to public funding for libel defendants.
legal_issues: Whether summary judgment was premature in the appellant's absence
Whether Article 6 required legal aid or a full trial
Appropriateness of sections 8-10 where defendant was unrepresented
Whether publication was real and substantial compared with Jameel
linked_authorities: Steinberg v Pritchard Englefield [2003] EWHC 1461 (QB)
Steel and Morris v United Kingdom (2005) 68416/01
Jameel v Dow Jones & Co Inc [2005] EWCA Civ 75

notes: Brief GMC interim suspension extension after doctor's imprisonment; Sullivan J extended order one year.

enrichment.short_title: R (GMC) v Baluchi: extension of interim suspension after imprisonment
key_facts: Dr Baluchi pleaded guilty to criminal offences and received a sentence of imprisonment.
The GMC sought judicial review to extend an interim order suspending his registration.
A fitness to practise hearing was listed for 29 March 2005 but practical difficulties arising from detention might prevent it proceeding.
Sullivan J considered a further year's suspension proportionate given the custodial sentence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application by the GMC to extend an interim suspension order pending fitness to practise proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Interim suspension extended for a further year until 3 March 2006.
enrichment.ratio: Where a doctor has been imprisoned following a guilty plea, extending interim suspension for a reasonable further period is proportionate to protect the public and allow alternative arrangements if listed proceedings cannot proceed.
legal_issues: Whether interim suspension should be extended pending full GMC hearing
Proportionality of a twelve-month extension where the doctor is detained
Practical effect of imprisonment on scheduled fitness to practise proceedings

notes: Pharmacy relocation JR; Deputy Judge dismissed Boots challenge to FHSAA preference for first-received Lloyds application.

enrichment.short_title: R (Boots) v FHSAA: competing pharmacy relocation applications at Biggleswade
key_facts: Boots and Lloyds both applied to relocate pharmaceutical services to a new Biggleswade health centre where only one provider could be approved.
Lloyds' application was received first; Boots later produced a Matrix Medical letter accepting its offer subject to PCT approval.
The PCT and FHSAA preferred Lloyds on a first-received basis, finding Boots had not secured confirmed control of the premises.
Boots challenged the decision for failure to apply Department of Health paragraph 76 guidance and alleged unfairness over a January 2004 Matrix letter not before the appeal body.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Family Health Services Appeal Authority decision dismissing Boots' appeal against refusal of its relocation application.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; Boots to pay FHSAA costs of £10,018.99; committee lawfully rejected Boots' control-of-premises argument and no procedural unfairness was established.
enrichment.ratio: Where competing pharmacy applications are otherwise equal, paragraph 76 guidance permits approval of the first received unless another deciding factor such as possession or likely control of premises is established; an appeal authority may reject a preferred-bidder letter conditioned on approval and need not consider evidence not put before it.
legal_issues: Application of paragraph 76 guidance on competing pharmacy applications
Whether Boots had secured control of the proposed premises
Procedural fairness regarding the January 2004 Matrix Medical letter
Whether Mr Burns' witness statement created unfairness

notes: Permission to appeal refused against strike-out of litigant-in-person conspiracy claim against council and police.

enrichment.short_title: Hare v Leeds City Council: permission refused on struck-out conspiracy claim
key_facts: Miss Hare, licensee of the World's End and freeholder of the Royal Oak in Pudsey, sued Leeds City Council and West Yorkshire Police alleging a conspiracy to damage her pub businesses.
She claimed customers were deterred by false statements, equipment sabotage and loss of staff linked to council redevelopment interests.
HHJ Grenfell struck out the claim under CPR 3.4 for disclosing no reasonable grounds and no factual basis.
Thomas J refused permission to appeal after hearing Miss Hare in person.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against a county court strike-out order in a human rights and conspiracy claim brought by a litigant in person.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; the judge's conclusion that the claim had no prospect of success was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Even where a litigant in person strongly believes a serious conspiracy against her business, CPR 3.4 strike-out is justified if the pleaded and oral case lacks any identifiable factual foundation capable of supporting Protocol 1 Article 1 or Article 8 claims.
legal_issues: Whether the claim disclosed reasonable grounds under CPR 3.4
Whether a litigant in person's oral amplification supplied missing factual basis
Appropriate approach to permission where human rights allegations are serious but unsupported

notes: Landmark ruling that section 6 HRA does not require exclusion of article 8 covert surveillance evidence; Button murder appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: R v Button: admissibility of covert police-station video obtained in breach of article 8
key_facts: Christina Button and Simon Tannahill were convicted of murdering Button's husband after a dog-walk attack motivated by debts and insurance gain.
Covert video of the defendants whispering at a police station was obtained after only audio surveillance had been authorised under RIPA, breaching article 8.
The prosecution case included circumstantial evidence and Tannahill's uncle's account of a prior request to find a killer.
The defence argued section 6 HRA made admission of article 8-breach evidence automatically unlawful.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and renewed application for leave to appeal against murder convictions raising a novel section 6 Human Rights Act point on evidence obtained by unauthorised covert video surveillance.
enrichment.outcome: Button's appeal dismissed and Tannahill's application refused; courts may admit relevant evidence obtained in breach of article 8 if fairness under article 6 and section 78 PACE permits.
enrichment.ratio: The breach of article 8 occurs at the point of covert surveillance, not when a court admits the evidence; section 6 does not require automatic exclusion because admissibility is governed by article 6 fairness and the section 78 discretion following Schenk, Khan and R v P.
legal_issues: Whether section 6 HRA prevents courts admitting article 8-breach evidence
Relationship between articles 6 and 8 in criminal trials
Effect of unauthorised RIPA surveillance on admissibility
Whether use of unlawfully obtained material repeats the article 8 breach
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference (No 2 of 2001) [2004] 2 AC 72
Khan v United Kingdom (2000) 31 EHRR 1016

notes: Tax sham-appeal JR; Jackson J held section 45(3) TMA 1970 does not require de novo rehearing after commissioner death.

enrichment.short_title: Hitch v Special Commissioners: continuation of tax appeal after commissioner's death
key_facts: Taxpayers appealed CGT assessments arising from a 1984 Singapore insurance scheme alleged by the Revenue to involve sham agreements.
Special Commissioners Everett and Shirley heard the appeal and found shams; the Court of Appeal restored that ruling and remitted the case in January 2001.
Commissioner Shirley died before the remitted appeals concluded; Hitch refused consent under section 45(3) to continue before Everett and Oliver QC.
Hitch sought a de novo rehearing to reopen the sham preliminary issue.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Special Commissioners' refusal to order a rehearing de novo after one commissioner's death and their direction to continue the remitted capital gains tax appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; section 45(3) is a quorum enabling provision and did not require taxpayer consent to continue the remitted appeals before a reconstituted panel.
enrichment.ratio: Section 45(3) of the Taxes Management Act 1970 regulates quorum and case management rather than stripping the Special Commissioners of jurisdiction to continue an appeal after a commissioner's death where the Court of Appeal has remitted the matter for further disposal.
legal_issues: Whether section 45(3) requires party consent to continue after a commissioner's incapacity
Effect of the Court of Appeal remittal order on the need for a fresh appeal
Whether taxpayer consent can force a de novo rehearing to reopen sham findings
Distinction between jurisdiction and case management on judge replacement
linked_authorities: Commissioners of Inland Revenue v TW Law Ltd [1950] 29 TC 467
Odhams Press Ltd v Cook [1938] 23 TC 233
R v Coates [2004] 1 WLR 3043

notes: AG reference on unduly lenient community sentence for causing death by careless driving; leave granted but sentence not increased.

enrichment.short_title: Attorney General's Reference No 157 of 2004: death by careless driving sentence
key_facts: A 22-year-old driver pleaded guilty to causing death by careless driving after a drunken night drive that killed his best friend Robert Cowie in a nearside collision on the A30.
Blood analysis showed about two-and-a-half times the permitted alcohol level and the driver was uninsured.
The Crown Court imposed a 240-hour community punishment order and a curfew order.
The deceased's mother expressed no desire for imprisonment and bore no ill will toward the offender.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging an unduly lenient non-custodial sentence for causing death by careless driving.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to refer granted because the sentence was unduly lenient in principle, but the court declined to substitute imprisonment given completion of most of the community order and exceptional mitigating circumstances.
enrichment.ratio: Causing death by careless driving with significant alcohol aggravation will usually warrant custody, but an unduly lenient community order may stand without increase where the offender has nearly completed it, double jeopardy applies, and the victim's family strongly oppose imprisonment.
legal_issues: Whether the community sentence was unduly lenient under section 36
Classification of the offence within Cooksley sentencing guidelines
Distinction from Attorney General's Reference No 77 of 2002 (Scotney)
Whether to increase sentence after substantial completion of community punishment
linked_authorities: R v Cooksley [2004] 1 Cr App R (S) 1
Attorney General's Reference No 77 of 2002 [2003] 1 Cr App R (S) 111
